speechtext:
Would the Minister of Justice care
to comment on a dispatch from Washington concerning a proposal in the house of representatives to make Canadian newsprint companies subject to United States anti-trust laws? Would it not be appropriate for our own combines investigation commissioner to inquire into the alleged monopolistic practices of this industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuari S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES ANTI-TRUST LAWS-QUESTION AS TO COMBINES INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
I wish to thank my hon. friend for having given me notice of this question. I have read the Washington dispatch reported in the Ottawa Journal of May 5 to which my hon. friend has just referred, and naturally have discussed this dispatch with the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. The situation alleged by Congressman Celler would have formed a possible subject for inquiry under the Havana charter for international trade organization had that charter been ratified by the United States of America, which sponsored it, and if as a consequence of United States ratification it had been ratified by other countries including Canada. The Havana charter, however, has not been ratified by the United States of America or by the other countries which are parties to it with, I believe, the single exception of Australia.
Our combines investigation commission has no jurisdiction to inquire formally into an international situation which does not
involve a combine detrimental to the Canadian public. Moreover, the effect of any information now before the Combines Investigation Act commissioner does not, in his opinion, justify an inquiry at the present time under our act into the newsprint industry. The information now before the combines investigation commission is that the Canadian newsprint industry is taking all reasonable steps to increase production, and that the prices Canadian newsprint producers are charging for sales of newsprint to the United States are exceptionally reasonable, having regard to the prices that could be obtained on the open market for newsprint at the present time if Canadian newsprint producers were to take full trading advantage of the present strong demand.
Under all the circumstances I do not think it would be desirable for me to comment further on a news dispatch to the effect that a subcommittee of a legislative body of another country has suggested the study of a bill to enforce the production of records of foreign countries.

DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE Defence forces-
245. To provide for the defence forces of the navy, army and air services and defence research and development, and to authorize total commitments for this purpose of $3,831,270,000 including authority notwithstanding section 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, to make commitments for the current year of $1,924,170,835 and commitments against future years of $1,907,099,165 against which commitments it is estimated that actual expenditures in 1951-52 will not exceed $1,595,050,000 of which 8183,050,000 will be provided from section 3 of the Defence Appropriation Act, 1950, as supplemented by item 246, $1,412,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, when the
committee rose last night I was answering some of the questions put to me by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The next question related to aircraft production, and the hon. member said that we had spent $30 million in 1950 but had not produced a plane that year. He asked why. He also said he did not know whether the F-86 had been produced yet, or whether any aircraft have been produced in addition to the two CF-100. The situation is, Mr. Chairman, that it takes a minimum of four years to develop a new type of aircraft, which was about the time taken in the case of the CF-100, the design of which began in the late months of 1946. From the time of having an aircraft that will
Supply-National Defence fly and that it is desirable to produce, it takes a minimum of eighteen months to begin production and to have the first aircraft ready. To tool up for the production of aircraft, I am informed, costs anywhere from $5 million to $30 million, depending upon the extent of the operation. In the case of an existing plant with floor space and basic machinery it might cost $5 million, and $30 million or more where all the machine tools have to be acquired.
It should be remembered that to produce one of these F-86E aircraft it takes about 25,000 man hours, and in the case of the CF-100 probably 40,000 or 50,000 man hours. The time laid down for the production of the F-86E, as announced by me when we placed the order, was met by the manufacturer with the production of the first of this type last year. They are now building up production, but it will still be some time before the planned rate of production is reached.
The CF-100 is a new type which is being entirely designed and developed here with a Canadian engine. It will go into production at the planned rate a little later than the F-86E. We expect that the planned rate of production on the F-86E will be reached during the summer or autumn of this year, and on the CF-100 early next year. I should point out that the performance in the production of the F-86E was really quite remarkable. This is an aircraft designed in. the United States. All the plans and a good many of the parts had to come from the United States. Like every new bit of complicated equipment it was subject to modification, and sometimes as many as ten a day would be sent up by air mail, telephone or telegraph. Notwithstanding that, the aircraft was completed within a very short time of the completion of the first corresponding aircraft in the United States-less than two weeks. Since then they have been going ahead very well.
The hon. member then said he was glad to see co-ordination between the three services, and the appointment of a chairman of the chiefs of staff committee in the person of Lieutenant General Foulkes. He asked what his duties were. They are to act as chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, which consists of the chiefs of staff and such other persons as the minister may designate; to coordinate training and operations of the Canadian forces; to perform such other duties as may be assigned to him by the minister.
The hon. member said there appears to be duplication in the three services, and that the

Supply-National Defence only important branch unified is the dental branch. He asked why we have three medical, nursing and hospital services. We have looked into the question of unifying the medical services a good many times over the last four years, but so far have decided against it primarily because of the principles I mentioned yesterday in connection with the unification of the motor vehicle maintenance service. Everything possible has been done to eliminate duplication. For example, the navy has four hospitals, at Halifax, Cornwallis, Esquimalt and Dartmouth respectively, each of which looks after army and air force personnel. The army has eleven hospitals, and four in conjunction with the Department of Veterans Affairs. All these hospitals look after navy and air force personnel. The R.C.A.F. has nine hospitals, all of which look after navy and army personnel. None of the services has a hospital at a place where any other service has a hospital, so there is no duplication. No country in the world, so far as I know, has the medical services combined into one.
Such a combination would have some desirable features, perhaps, but on the other hand there would be a loss of direct association with the traditions and work of each particular service. We would soon have a joint medical service having specialists for the army, specialists for the navy, and specialists for the air force. The advantages of unification, therefore, would not be nearly as great as might be expected. Further, there would be administrative difficulties in deciding to which officer this neutral medical service would be responsible. Experience has shown it is necessary that a directorate be responsible to a single officer, not to a committee or to the minister. The only practicable way of doing that, in the light of experience, would appear to be to put the medical services of the navy and air force under the control of the largest user and the one having the greatest need under actual service conditions, the army; and that might not please the navy or the air force because they believe they have special functions, too. While the matter is continuing to receive very close attention, it has not yet been decided to do this job. I repeat to the hon. member and to the house that, so far as I know, this course has not been decided upon by any country.
The next question was: Is there duplication of supplies? The army provides stores and food for the air force and, to a considerable degree, for the navy. The rations are the same. The purchasing is all done through the Department of Defence Production and we do not see that there would be any elimination

of services or any economy effected through unifying the supply services. It would probably mean the setting up of a new overhead organization to look after the supply services of all three.
May I say >to the minister that what prompted the question was my impression that the bill for printing for the services was rather high; I refer to the printing of papers.
All the printing for the armed services is obtained through the king's printer, and he 'places the contracts.
I refer to stationery.

I am afraid there is a good deal of paper work in connection with modern forces. We are trying to cut down on it; but the larger they get, the more paper work there is. It is like a telephone system; the larger it is, the more connections there are. I found recently that there were twenty-two forms required to document each recruit. I had an investigation made in an effort to cut down the number; and so far as I can make out, they feel now that they need one more. But seriously we are trying to cut down this work.
The hon. member stated that there is no common attestation form. The reason for that is that each of the three services-the navy, the army and the air force-feels that on attestation they require information peculiar to their particular service. Hence, in the light of their present attitude, to have a common form would mean having a bigger form so that you could cover all the ground in the navy, the army and the air force.
The army has lately instituted a completely new form of revolutionary design. It is designed to be a self-contained file. It has the carbon paper inserted. It has the recruit's medical report, enrolment, personnel selection report, oath and so on, all included. This is designed to expedite and simplify the work of enrolment. It is being used now for the first time in Canada; and the navy and the air force are watching with close interest to see if this is the right kind of form to have. We are therefore looking into the matter. We are also working on drawing up a uniform medical profile along the lines of the army pulhem, for all three services, so that any examining officer or personnel officer could examine men and code them for placement in the army, the navy or the air force according to their qualifications, physical, mental and so on. That is being done. It is a rather large undertaking, because in the three services there are no less than five

hundred or more separate classifications of jobs that have to be related one to the other; for instance, you have to find what is the air force equivalent in requirements for an engine room artificer, and so on. That work is being pressed on. So far as I know, it is greatly in advance of work being done anywhere else.
The hon. member referred to the size of the reserve force as shown in the statement at page 88 of the report of the department for the year ended March 31, 1950. The reserve force has been built up steadily since the war. During the last three years the increase as shown in the white paper-and I am speaking from recollection-would be 44 per cent. It is bigger now than it was in the period immediately following the second world war. We have tried every means suggested, I believe, except exemption from income tax and compulsory service, in order to expedite this build-up. We have had great co-operation. The fact that it should have increased by more than one-third has been, I say, most encouraging indeed. We hope that increase will continue.
But our aim during this period has not been to have a reserve force in the army that is trained and ready to fight a trained enemy. That is not yet part of the role of the reserve army of Canada; and I think that a great deal of misunderstanding occurs because of that misconception. What we want to do is to have the organization, the armouries, the equipment, the procedure, the regimental traditions, the officers, and so far as possible the N.C.O.'s, on which to build rapidly. The aim during this period has been to have 100 per cent of officers, about 75 per cent of N.C.O.'s and about 50 per cent of men. We have come close to achieving that aim with regard to officers and N.C.O.'s, and we are not far off with regard to men. While we want to see more men in the reserve force, and to give them every possible kind of encouragement and assistance, there is no ground for the kind of talk of despair and discouragement that we sometimes hear either in the House of Commons or in its committees. Relatively, our reserve army is in a better position, from the point of view of officer qualification, N.C.O. qualification, armouries and equipment, than it has ever been before; and I believe it is better off than the territorial army in England or the national guard in the United States-that is, on a comparative basis. I believe it would help in building up the reserve if we recognize, as I do every time I see them,-and I see them probably more than does any other hon.
Supply-National Defence member-the magnificent job they are doing, and give them every encouragement and every assistance.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin said that he was told that Canadair could produce ten F-86E's a day, and he asked why we should not do it. We have made arrangements with the United States for the supply to us of all government-found property that is to go into the F-86E's that they can deliver to us, at a cost of approximately $175,000 per aircraft. I may say that the allocation at first made by them was only just over half what we persuaded them to give or to sell us today; and what they are providing today out of their own resources, because there is not enough of this special equipment-engines, instruments and the like-to go round. They are short of them. We are making, or we shall be making when we reach the planned rate of production, all the F-86E's for which there will be engines and other equipment available. The suggestion that we should produce ten a day is an interesting one, because I think hon. members should know about what it would cost. Ten a day would be, we estimate, about $4 million a day, of which $1,750,000 would be paid to the United States. That would mean a total of $1,200 million a year; and that would of course mean having to provide for the expenditure in some way or another, by doubling or tripling the present income tax or by some other means of that kind, which would have a most inflationary effect. That rate of production would be beyond the peacetime capacity of this country, and, indeed, beyond that of any country of comparable size. The planned rate of production is within our capacity and within the budget.
Then the hon. member said: We should have started our three-year program three years ago. We have had a three-year program ever since 1947, and each year we have revised it in the light of the progress made and of the international situation; so that it has been a steady development in accordance with lines laid down three and even four years ago, but with a great acceleration.
Then he said: There should be more diversification of defence installations. I think there he suggests we should have a greater spread across the country. I do not know of any government activity where there is greater diversification. For example, much the largest concentration of defence activity is in Nova Scotia. In 1950-51 in the maritimes alone, where there is 9-30 per cent of the population, 14-10 per cent of the defence dollar was spent. In the prairies, as I have informed the house, we are opening or

Supply-National Defence re-opening some eight major establishments, so that in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta we will be spending again a very considerable amount in proportion to the population.
Then the hon. member said: It is a crime that men serving in our armed forces and fighting for us should have to pay income tax. That is a question for the Minister of Finance, which he will deal with when he has material before the house if it is considered desirable; but I should point out that we in the Department of National Defence consider it very much fairer to have all personnel pay income tax. If they were relieved from income tax a major general would be relieved of a payment of $172.30 a month, whereas a first-class private would be relieved of a payment of $6.85 a month. We believe that the differentiation in responsibility between the private and the major general is correctly measured by the pay scales, and should not be further added to by exemption from income tax.
Why could not the ceiling on income tax exemption be that allowed to the private?

It would affect your whole pay scale, which has been very carefully worked out. In the second world war it was found at one stage that it was possible that ten different men, each with a wife and two children, could be on a voyage from Halifax, Nova Scotia, to St. John's, Newfoundland, and these ten men would pay ten separate income taxes on the same rates of pay for doing equivalent work. It is exceedingly difficult to make exemptions and to make differentiations. At what stage would you start exempting the men? Would it be at Fort Lewis? Would it be at Tokyo? Would it be back in the line? Would it apply to the army service corps, to lines of communication, to the private in the front ranks?
You have to decide that point in connection with 'the application of veterans benefits.

It is a tough one, and so far the view of the government is this: it is a good principle that everyone should pay income tax, and that any differentiation in service or responsibility should be compensated for directly in pay which everyone can see.
The hon. member for Trinity-Conception asked if any other ships could be stationed in Newfoundland, and could there be more defence preparations there. The answer is that Newfoundland comes within the zone of Canada-United States defence plans, ties in with the over-all planning for defence of

both countries on the Atlantic coast, and future plans do envisage the stationing of additional ships in Newfoundland. But I point out that to do it at present would add greatly to the shore-based facilities needed in Newfoundland, and to the cost of operations, so that it is much better that ships exercising in the Atlantic should continue to be based at Halifax so long as the operations stay on their present scale.
The hon. member for Calgary East asked: How many fighter squadrons are ready for defence of. this country now? That is the kind of question we do not give answers to, but the number will increase very rapidly as the new aircraft are produced. At the present time we have fighters equipped with Vampires and Mustangs, which are both good operational aircraft, but not nearly up to the class of the F-86E and the CF-100. Just as soon as they are available they will be issued to equip squadrons that will be trained and ready to receive them. The build-up will come along together, and without giving any information about which there should be security, it is quite obvious from the size of operations that Canadair Limited or A. V. Roe Canada Limited by the end of this year will be producing enough aircraft of the F-86E or CF-100 type to equip a squadron every month, approximately. I should think that would be a fair estimate.
Then the hon. member said: We have airborne battalions, but they are not trained together, and we have not the transport to carry them. Well, they are trained together as battalions. They have been trained together with supporting arms as battalions, but not as a brigade group, and it is not considered at this stage that they would be employed as a brigade group. However, they will receive combined training so that they can fit into the larger formations if that action is needed. The hon. member said: We have not the transport to carry them. I suppose he is thinking in terms of something like the C-119 of the United States. Neither has any other country except the United States. Plans provide for our acquiring some of these aircraft later, but we believe that priority in respect of aircraft can be regarded as first, fighters, second, bombers-we are not going to have any strategic bombers- third, tactical fighters; fourth, transport-and that includes of course transport of troops. We have a sufficient number of equipped North Stars and Dakotas to make an airlift of the kind which at the present we would envisage as being required.
Then the hon. member referred to the fact that in a speech on February 5 there was only one sentence referring to the reserve

forces. I do not suppose that is a very-serious comment. Throughout the year I suppose I have spoken to a hundred or more audiences in support of the reserve forces, and visited every reserve force unit that I have had time to visit, so as to give them every possible support and assistance.
The hon. member expressed the view that my reports on the reserve forces were too optimistic. I believe in giving people encouragement and praise when they deserve it. And I think we have carried into effect every suggestion made by the defence association or by the individual associations or branches of the reserve forces, except that regarding conscription and exemption from income tax; and as I say I am all in favour of their being exempt from income tax. However, neither myself nor anyone else has been able to find a way which would enable the Minister of Finance and the government to do it without finding some new principle, without providing for a special class in a special way, without calling something which is income not income. If somebody can suggest a way in which that can be done, then I will certainly bring it to the attention of my colleagues.
How was it done in the last war?	'

In the last war we had about twelve scales of income tax, depending on whom you were serving with, where you were serving, and what you were doing. Our practice now is to have just one scale of income tax applicable to everyone, wherever he is serving and whatever he is doing.
The hon. member said that anti-tank regiments have had their weapons taken away. It is quite true that some armoured regiments have had some of their weapons used in a different way. We have taken away some of the tanks on issue to units to put them in shape for shipment abroad, where they would be closer to the fighting line. But in every case we have replaced them either with equivalent weapons mounted on carriers, or towed twenty-five pounders, which has enabled the training in the army to be carried on. Training out in the field is still carried on with tanks, whether the training is local or at a central camp.
The hon. member said there is no information that equipment will be replaced soon by United States weapons. We have sent two divisions of equipment abroad. Our expectation is that delivery of the equipment to replace the first will begin within the next two weeks. In view of the general 80709-1841
Supply-National Defence situation in the world, that is an exceedingly good arrangement to make with the United States authorities.
The member said that the minister had made no statement as to how we are to replace equipment half of which we have disposed of. This is to be replaced from the United States or out of our own manufacture later.
He said that some of the United States equipment is not as good-the Bren gun as compared with the Browning, the twenty-five pounder as compared with the 105, and moreover, the cost is very much higher. That is a matter of opinion. You could not persuade an American of that fact. And, so far as one can see, from the advice I have received from my officials the difference in these weapons is very little.
He said that the adoption of uniform weapons would be of far greater advantage to the United States. There is the question of the Sten and the Thompson. Here, however, I think the hon. member is entering a field which is different, the field of hand-arms. So long as these weapons use the same ammunition

and I believe that is true of the Sten-it may be quite possible to keep the Sten, which is a much cheaper weapon, and not take the Thompson. That is receiving consideration.
The hon. member referred to overhead, with too many men not fighting, and the setup being top-heavy. As I have said, I think we have the lowest overhead of any of our partners outside the iron curtain, referring to operational troops in proportion to the total. And I believe that if a study is made on a comparable basis it will be found that our divisional slice is smaller than that of any comparable country. It seems to me that there may be a new principle we have discovered in this, and that is that the overhead goes up, not down, with the size of the force.
The hon. member for Yale said that the reserve force lacked funds, particularly for certain purposes, and that they were operating in cramped quarters and housed in school buildings. The -accommodation for the reserve army has been increased by over one hundred per cent in the last five years, and we are doing everything possible to continue this increase as rapidly as we can, having regard always to other requirements which are considered more urgent. As far as I can recall there has been no suggestion from representatives of the reserve force that their funds should be increased again. Substantial changes have been made over the last three years.
The hon. member said that the personnel are not receiving rehabilitation grants. There

Supply-National Defence was never any suggestion that the reserve force should receive rehabilitation grants.
I have never heard that suggestion from anyone.
The hon. member said we should remove the bottleneck preventing defence activities over the highway between Alberta and British Columbia, and the highway between Kamloops and Vancouver. I have made inquiries of the general staff and find that they do not regard these as urgent military requirements.
He said that we should develop airfields at Grand Forks, Kamloops, and other points. We are developing all the airfields we need at the present time, or that we can afford to have at this time, and we are establishing them in the places which in our opinion are best suited for air-training, namely in the prairie provinces, where we will have eight additional airfields in operation, as soon as the work can be done.
The hon. member referred to civil defence, a matter which comes under the supervision of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who will speak about this at a later time.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said there was no brigade training area or camp in the maritime provinces, and that there was too much centralization. I have answered the question about centralization as it applies to defence establishments. I can tell him that we are looking for an area in the maritime provinces which will be suitable for large-scale training. At present the only two in Canada are at Petawawa and Wainwright, and both of them have cold winters and a good deal of snow. If in the maritime provinces we could find an area of more than one hundred square miles of suitable ground, which could be acquired at no great cost and without displacing too many people, and also with no valuable standing timber on it, we should be glad indeed to consider it. We have had officers looking into this matter since 1946, but they have not yet found a suitable area.
Xhe hon. member referred to the question of men abroad not receiving dependents allowances. This was answered in the house on March 18, as reported at page 1373 of Hansard. We have tried to build up pay schedules by having pay rates which are equivalent to those in the eight leading industries of Canada, so that it will be unnecessary to have dependents allowances again. Should, however, the necessity become evident, that certainly must be considered.
The hon. member for Broadview said the reserve army should train as complete units. We believe that at the outset it is much
more useful for the reserve army to go to camp and do individual training or sub-unit training, having all their housekeeping looked after for them. In this way the days they spend in camp can be spent in intensive training in weapons. That has been the view since the second world war, and that procedure will be carried on. However, as units achieve a standard in individual training where they can profit from unit training, then I agree with him completely. I can see also the advantage in having the unit, from the administrative and traditional points of view, and from the point of view of morale. As we pass through this period of acquiring trained officers, trained N.C.O.'s and a nucleus of trained men, we will do more along the lines of his suggestion.
The hon, member suggested there should be danger pay up in the front line. This is something they have had in the United States but, I think, not in other forces. The Canadian government has always been opposed to it. I think Canada's armed forces have been opposed to it. However, we are doing something in that regard. We pay an additional allowance to men abroad of $9 a month for privates, $12 for sergeants, $15 for W.0.2's and $16.50 for W.O.l's. So far $47,000 has been paid in this way to the forces in Korea.
The hon. member for Vegreville asked if it would not be possible for us to take in other than British subjects. I should say that an amendment was passed on March 16, 1951, to K.R. Canada concerning the qualifications for enrolment which now read:
(a) be a Canadian citizen or other British subject; except that the minister may authorize the enrolment of a citizen of another country that is a party to the North Atlantic treaty if he is satisfied that the national interest would not be prejudiced thereby and if such enrolment is not prohibited by the law of such country.
As you can see, it is pretty restricted for security reasons. I must say that my military advisers are very strongly of the view that we should limit our armed forces to Canadian citizens or other British subjects. The same practice is followed in most countries. In Canada we are in a peculiar position in that we have a considerable proportion of our population of United States origin. They are just as loyal to the same causes as we are. We both move freely across the common border, and we thought it would be desirable to make some exception in their case, and other similar cases. After all, the twelve nations of the North Atlantic treaty are all in it together as partners, and we should accept each other's nationals in our services in so far as that can be safely done. I can tell the hon. member that that is the situation, If it

should be desirable to extend it, then we shall be very glad indeed to give the matter further consideration.
The hon. member for Three Rivers referred to the small number of French speaking officers in the three services. There is nothing I should like to see more than a larger proportion of officers of French origin in the three services. However, I do not agree that just because we do not have them we should promote men of any race who have not the required qualifications of experience, education or military bearing. It would be very desirable indeed if we could secure a larger proportion of men who were originally French speaking, and who would have the desire to make the service a career. At the present -time we are doing very well at Royal Military College and Royal Roads. Twenty-five per cent of the cadets are of French speaking origin, and a good proportion of those are making the services their career. That is fine, and we would like to see more of them. But there is a considerable handicap involved in the service of a French speaking officer in the armed forces due to the fact that it is quite impossible to keep him -and his family located in a community predominantly French and Catholic. When he moves away to secure promotion, to take a course or to take on some other job, then he is faced with the alternatives of either leaving his family behind in the community of relatives and friends who speak their tongue, or taking them with him to a community that may be predominantly Protestant and English.
I can mention cases that have come to my attention. In the course of promotion an officer with the rank of major in the army was transferred from the ordnance depot at Montreal east to a senior position at Calgary or Edmonton. He was faced with the necessity of taking his children from a French speaking Catholic school to an English speaking Catholic school, and his wife from the community of their friends to one where very few people spoke their language.
We speak French in Calgary.

Not all of you. One can understand the difficulties. It is a real difficulty, but I can assure the hon. member who brought up the matter that it is one which has our complete and understanding sympathy, and that we are doing everything possible to overcome it. In opening R.M.C. a couple of years ago I referred to this question particularly, and perhaps I might read a passage from my speech. I said:
Since my appointment I have emphasized the importance of a knowledge of both English and French to all Canadians, but particularly those of
Supply-National Defence the armed forces. Obviously an officer possessing both languages has an advantage in exercising leadership and command, in getting along with his fellows in peace or war, in access to additional knowledge and in work as liaison officers, military attaches and the like. The knowledge of both languages is a positive military advantage. Accordingly, French and English are both compulsory subjects at both colleges for the first three years. That, however, is not enough. I urge staffs and cadets to see to it that by one means or another they learn to speak both languages fluently before the end of their course.
In point of fact, as to every promotion list that is put before me for consideration I ask the officer concerned, the chief of staff of the service or his representative, expressly if there is not a French-speaking officer within the range of qualifications who,, despite seniority, can be promoted. The fact: is that the gaps sometimes are too big to be bridged. For example, at the present time we have two brigadiers in. the army who are-very distinguished officers. They are both destined for high places. They have magnificent war records and are relatively young. One is eleventh and the other is twelfth in in the list of brigadiers. One has seventeen years' service and the other thirteen. To promote them to major generals at the present time would be unfair to them because they would reach the -age of retirement, through having achieved and- held the highest possible ranks, before they had acquired sufficient pension to justify their retirement. These officers are doing very good work indeed. One is at the imperial war college in London, having exercised command in Quebec. The other is the deputy chief of the general staff in Ottawa. One of them is destined to be in command in Montreal very shortly. But at present Major General Morton is in command in Montreal, and he speaks French, but one of these officers will be transferred there on General Morton's retirement. I am afraid we simply cannot run three services the size of ours if we do not see to it that we make the best of our racial and linguistic position. I regard it as a positive asset that we should have officers of both languages in all three services, and I should like to see more of them.
The hon. member also suggested that a military college should be established at Quebec city. That has been considered, and we do not exclude it at all. At present, however, the cost of the other two colleges is very considerable indeed, and we are most happy to have the proportion of twenty-five per cent French-speaking students mixed in with the English-speaking students at Kingston and Royal Roads. We hope it will have a good influence in making both groups better Canadians.

Supply-National Defence
The hon. member suggested that we should have ships manned exclusively with Frenchspeaking officers and men. That might be desirable if we had a very much larger navy, but with our navy, which has a present strength of about 14,000, it is not economically possible to do so, even if it were desirable; therefore I am afraid we cannot do it.
I think the only remaining suggestion made was that of the hon. member for Peel with respect to the St. Lawrence waterway. We regard this as a defence project of immense importance and would like to see it proceeded with, if possible jointly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I intend to speak very briefly, not so much on national defence as in order to correct a statement which, if permitted to go uncorrected, might have an effect on reserve recruiting. Yesterday afternoon I listened to most of the speech by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, but I was not in the chamber at the time he made this comment, which appears at page 2858 of Hansard:
That man has a job: he is in a certain income tax bracket. If he joins the reserve army he will be paid $20 or $25 a month, which must be added to his income. That puts him in another income tax bracket. At the end of the year, instead of the reserve army paying him something, he pays Mr. Abbott something. He really loses in the transaction: he has drilled for nothing, because the money is taken back in income tax.
I want to start by saying that the hon. member is generally pretty well informed on his subject matter, but when I am through I think he will agree that in this case he was in error. It is quite a common mistake in this country to presume that when you cross into another income tax bracket somehow or other you are in danger of losing net income. I want to say quite flatly, before I give some examples I have prepared, that under our income tax system it is impossible for any person to work for extra income and suffer a loss of net income. Our income tax tables are designed to avoid that.
I am going to take one or two very simple examples which would apply to men in the reserve army. As hon. members know, in Canada a single man gets an exemption of $1,000 and a married man with no children an exemption of $2,000 from income tax. On the first thousand dollars of income beyond that in both cases the rate is 15 per cent, and most of these young reservists will be in that income tax bracket. This extra $20 a month, if it does not take him into the next bracket, as normally it would not, will be subject to tax at the rate of 15 per cent, or 18 per cent with the new surtax. So he will pay exactly the same tax as he paid before on his basic income, and in addition he will pay 18 per cent on the $20 or $3.60 a month, leaving

him $16.40 tax free out of his additional earnings. That applies to both single and married men in the first income tax bracket. Let us suppose, whether he be single or married, he is right at the top of his bracket; that is a single man earning $2,000 or a married man earning $3,000, so the extra $20 a month he gets from the reserve army does carry him into the next bracket. In that bracket "the tax is 17 per cent, but payable not on his entire income but only on the next thousand dollars. So he pays exactly the same income tax on his ordinary income, and on the extra $20 he pays 17 per cent plus the 20 per cent surtax or a total of 20-4 per cent. Therefore he pays the same basic income tax on his other income as he paid before. On this extra income, this $20 a month, he pays $4.08, and has roughly $16 left tax free.
I will even go to the extreme case, to show how it is impossible for any person to work more and suffer a loss in net income. Take one of those few but happy individuals in the very top income tax bracket, over $400,000 a year. In this bracket the tax is 80 per cent. Suppose he joined the reserve army and was paid this extra $20 a month. He would continue to pay his ordinary tax on his basic income. On the extra $20 he would pay 80 per cent plus the new defence surtax, making 96 per cent, so he would still have 80 cents left over and above his former net income. Of course in that case he would hardly be joining because of the incentive of $20. That leads me to the other point, which is based upon a statement made recently by the deputy minister of national defence. The small material incentive which would be given by cancellation of income tax on this reserve pay is not sufficient to induce any extra recruiting, in the opinion of the deputy minister given just last week. Again I repeat, just to correct any misapprehension which might have gone abroad, that a recruit in the reserve army cannot possibly lose financially by joining up, no matter what his base income may be and no matter what brackets he may cross. Certainly in low brackets he will have the great bulk of his extra income left to him, in addition to his ordinary net income.
I do not intend to speak on the question of income tax on those in the armed services, because the Minister of National Defence has pointed out that the Minister of Finance will deal with that matter when the income tax resolutions are before the house. I have been reminded, however, that in the years before I was a parliamentary assistant I made a speech on this matter when I was just home from overseas, and it reads very much like the speech made by the hon. member for Broadview yesterday. I have not changed

my opinion very much on that matter. I think the proper way to pay for the extra hazard or danger of front line service is not by the remission of income tax but by extra combat pay. That was the American practice, and in my experience it was the British practice. In R.A.F. service in Libya we did get extra pay not only for the theatre of operations but also to make up for the fact that our living quarters and food certainly were not the same as those of the soldier back at base or in Canada. I suggest that the proper attack to be made on this problem is not by suggesting the remission of tax. The Minister of National Defence put his finger squarely on the issue. When you talk about the remission of income tax for those in the armed services it is not the private you are going to help; it is the high ranking officer. If the difference in what the private soldier would pay in income tax were regarded as the base for combat pay, I suggest that combat pay would be a very small item indeed. However, that point will be dealt with by the Minister of Finance when the budget resolutions are considered. All I want to do is emphasize that under our taxation system it is impossible for anyone, soldier or worker, who chooses to work extra hours to earn extra income to be left as a consequence with less net income. He cannot help but gain if he works more.

I was very interested in what the parliamentary assistant just said with regard to combat pay and related subjects. I had not intended to deal with that in my remarks this afternoon, but since the hon. member has raised the question I just want to say that like him and probably every other member here who had the privilege of serving in either of the two wars, I think the feeling is universal that the proper man to receive trades pay or extra pay, if extra pay is to be given for extra service, is the man who carries the rifle, the man who operates the gun in the aircraft, or who mans the gun on the fighting ship.
I know this is a difficult subject, but by the very nature of things skilled tradesmen- probably not from their own choice-have to work under conditions and circumstances where they are not near the actual battle front. As a result trades pay is much more prevalent in rear areas and workshop areas. I do not deny there is danger in some of those areas, but as a rule trades pay is more concentrated in areas where the danger is not great than in danger areas, where there is little trades pay. I certainly feel this subject is one that requires careful consideration. Now that our troops are once more in actual
Supply-National Defence battle, I think we might give some consideration to whether the trained rifleman should not receive some form of trades pay. I should think it would be possible to work out some scheme under which a man who qualifies to meet certain tests as a first-class infantryman with a rifle battalion, and similarly in the other services, should receive something in recognition of that fact. If it is right to give trades pay to a man who is trained to maintain vehicles, I think we might consider whether we should not also give trades pay to men trained in maintaining their profession as fighting soldiers.
It is quite obvious from thte discussion that has gone on so far that all parties in the house are in agreement on the need for an expanded and accelerated national defence program. But the agreement on goals need not, and in my view should not, preclude honest disagreement on methods and interim objectives. No one denies that all the free nations are in peril of momentary Russian aggression. No one in this house denies the necessity for the enlarged defence program, and the raising of additional forces recently outlined by the minister. It is not correct to say, however, that to question either the adequacy of the over-all program or the efficacy of the methods being followed is in any way to impede the war effort. Such an argument I reject absolutely. What is needed is a measured examination of the whole program as announced, to see if it is adequate to meet the peril, and to see whether the methods being followed will, in fact, enable accomplishment of the program laid down by the government. If we believe there are doubts on either score, we must say so. National defence is too serious to fool around with. Personally, I have doubts on both scores.
First, as to whether the program announced by the government is adequate to meet the requirements of the situation: I intend to make no criticism at this time of the extent of the commitments presently laid down by the government which may be generally summarized as being, in the army, two brigades for overseas-one in Korea and one for Europe-and one airborne brigade for home defence; for the air force, forty operational squadrons, of which eleven are destined for Europe; in the navy, a general force of one hundred active ships. Whether or not that figure is intended to be one hundred fighting ships, I have not yet been able to gather from the minister's statements. If there were one hundred fighting ships, then we are obviously going to have many more ships than that in service in the navy, but the only figure it is safe to mention at this

Supply-National Defence time is the one hundred ships in commission in the navy when our objective is reached.
I fear that it will not be possible adequately to fulfil and maintain these commitments within the limitations -now governing our forces, that is the limitation of 115,000 service personnel by 1954. I believe it will be found either that the commitment must be reduced or the number of personnel increased, or we shall run the danger once again of inadequate support for our forces when they are engaged in operations.
Before stating my reasons in detail for this criticism, I think it is interesting to take a general look at our military commitments in terms of those of other countries, particularly of the United States. As I said, at this time I am making no -criticism of the size and the extent of our commitment. But I think it does help us to keep a sense of perspective when we are discussing national defence just to look at the extent of the commitment of our ally. I realize also it is not strictly accurate to say, because another country has a population ten times that of our own, that we should necessarily, therefore, be able to put forth an exactly proportionate war effort, that is one-tenth of theirs, because there are many other factors which intervene. But when we are comparing population figures, it does seem to me it is an indication of the proportional effor of the two countries.
When we are considering this matter then, we find that the United States, with a population approximately ten times that of Canada, has as its goal of serving personnel in the armed forces-I understand that is what we would call active forces and does not include the national guard-3,500,000 men. According to my understanding they expect to reach that goal this year. Our active service personnel on a strictly proportionate basis would be one-tenth of that number or 350,000. Now, I have said that a strictly proportional relationship may not be possible because the United States has admittedly a more developed economy, but in terms of serving personnel it is an indication. We must bear in mind the fact that our goal is 115,000 service personnel by 1954; that is, our target is something less than one-third of what it would be if we were to achieve a goal on a basis exactly proportionate to that of the United States. And that in three years' time.
Then, Mr. Chairman, for the purpose of a detailed consideration of whether we can meet our commitments within the target strength of 115,000 service personnel, it is interesting to compare our effort and

strength in the last war with our announced commitments and proposed strength under the present program. If you will remember, Mr. Chairman, during the recent war Canada had five divisions in the field as a fighting force, three infantry divisions, two armoured divisions and two independent armoured brigades. Taking the equivalent of three brigades per division, that is either infantry or armoured brigades, and the equivalent of a brigade of artillery, one might say roughly that you had four brigades per division or that five divisions would give you the equivalent of twenty brigades plus the two armoured brigades which would make twenty-two. In making this comparison, I think it is only proper to bear in mind, of course, that there were reconnaissance regiments, as well as corps troops, who actually did fight although they were not included in any of the divisions or independent brigades.
I believe it would be a fairly generous estimate, and would form a fair basis of comparison, instead of taking twenty-two, the strict mathematical computation, to say we had the equivalent of thirty brigades within our five divisions and two independent brigades when we include reconnaissance, corps -and army fighting troops. During the war of 1939-1945 to maintain a fighting force equal to thirty brigades took 495,804 men. Then three brigades, which is our present commitment, on the same basis would take approximately 49,580 men to maintain them. That figure of 49,580 would mean that the army alone would require a strength of nearly half the total planned strength of 115,000 which is to cover all three services.
Actually there has been an announcement that it is the intention of the government, with respect to the brigade for Europe, to rotate that brigade on -a basis which the minister outlined. You cannot, therefore, just look for a brigade for Europe. Leaving out altogether the necessity of reinforcing either the brigade for Korea or the brigade for Europe, should hostilities occur there, we are committed to that rotation of the force. I believe I am correct in saying that at no time during the last war were we ever committed to a policy of complete rotation of service personnel. Since we are going to have to rotate the brigade in Europe, it would automatically follow that in fairness some provision will have to be made for rotating -the brigade in Korea. You cannot, therefore, just take a figure of three brigades. It seems to me you have to take a figure of

more like five brigades which we shall have to be able to maintain on the basis of the commitment the minister has laid down.
On a comparative basis-and although this I admit is not strictly accurate nevertheless it forms a basis on which to judge-taking the figures as to what it took to maintain that number of brigades during the 1939-45 war, to maintain five brigades or their equivalent at this time would take approximately 80,000 men. That is, I repeat, for the army alone.
When we come to the air force, a similar comparison is even more startling. It has been announced that our program calls for 40 squadrons. During the last war, at its peak, according to official figures which I have been given, the air force had the equivalent of 78 operational squadrons. That figure was reached in 1943. At that time, again according to the official figures, the air force's maximum strength was 209,803. Here, of course, comparisons are perhaps even more difficult to make; but I think that a comparison should be made for the purpose of discussion.
During the last war we had a number of bomber squadrons. I understand that we are to have no heavy bomber squadrons under the program now envisaged, so that one would have to make adjustments for that differential, as a bomber squadron takes a much higher proportion of men than does a fighter squadron. The official air force figures show however that even with the bomber squadrons overseas only approximately one-third of the air force personnel overseas was engaged in bomber activities. We therefore do not need to weight the comparison too heavily as a result of the fact that this time we eliminate the bomber squadrons. On the basis of a straight mathematical comparison, if there were 78 squadrons at the peak of strength, and a total of 209,800 men to maintain that number of squadrons, therefore 40 squadrons-again on a straight mathematical basis-can be said to need 117,000 men. That is for the air force alone.
Let us for the purpose of argument make a heavy cut because there are to be no bomber squadrons under the program that is now envisaged. Suppose you want to take a third off that figure. That still leaves between
75,000	and 80,000 which might be considered as being required to maintain that 40 squadrons, unless we are to say that the use of manpower during the last war was excessively prodigal. There are, of course, other reasons why the comparison must be carefully made. We are going to have only 11
Supply-National Defence squadrons overseas at this time, whereas a large portion of our effort last time was in Europe.
But, Mr. Chairman, we are committed to keeping 11 squadrons in Europe under this program, and again, since the intention has been announced of rotating army personnel in Europe, I can only presume that, in fairness, the same intention would apply with respect to air force personnel. You are therefore committed to an 11-squadron force in Europe on a rotation basis; so that even if it is necessary to be extremely careful in making your comparison between these figures and the figures of the last war, because of the absence this time of a bomber effort, nevertheless your figures are weighted back again because you are committed to maintaining a substantial part of your force in Europe on a rotational basis.
Taking then the mathematical calculations alone, one would have a figure of some
190,000	men for the army and the air force, on a comparative basis. Giving it then all the care and the weight which must be attached to the fact that our effort is not as all-out at the present time as it was in wartime, nevertheless I think it is quite safe to say that the ceiling of 115,000, if it is not going to be exceeded-and I would certainly think that it will have to be exceeded-would certainly have to be stretched to the limit to maintain the commitments to the extent outlined for the army and air force alone; and the figures that I have given take no account of our naval effort.
In this connection I think we should also consider the physical problem of actual reinforcements. We have to bear in mind the fact that our men are fighting a war in Korea. For international political purposes it may be called police action or it may be called the restraint of aggression. It makes no difference what political name we give to it; to the men on the spot it is a war; and by anyone dealing with the problem of maintaining that force and reinforcing that brigade, it must be dealt with on the basis of a war. One is therefore surely entitled to look, and should do so, at the figures of the last war for some basis of comparison. Official figures for a comparable theatre can be found in the figures of casualties during the Italian campaign during the last war. I think that Italy would be a more comparable theatre than northwest Europe because of the factors of disease and so on, which would be more nearly similar in the case of Italy and Korea than they would be in the case of northwest Europe and Korea.

Supply-National Defence
The figure for our non-battle casualties for the Canadian component of the allied army in Italy for one year, namely 1944-and I point out that these are non-battle casualties alone-was 38,973. The approximate average monthly strength of the Canadian component was 72,000. So that of the total average strength in the theatre for a year, one-half were non-battle casualties. The rate of casualties of all types-that is, battle as well as non-battle casualties-was 61 per 1,000 per month which, it would seem to me, means a figure of 720 over a 12-month period. With the casualty figures being worked out on this basis, and that is the only way we can arrive at it, it would seem that 720 or seven-tenths would be casualties, either battle or nonbattle, in the course of a 12-month period. The provision for reinforcements must surely be based on the anticipated casualty rate, which must take in casualties from all sources and when you look at the figures for the last war, you can see that the problem of reinforcing the Korean brigade is a heavy one indeed, when you realize that in Italy the non-battle casualties for a year amounted to a total of one-half of the total actual strength in the theatre.
In this connection there is an interesting statement by Brigadier Rockingham, commander of the Canadian brigade in Korea, as reported in a Canadian Press dispatch which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of April 19. It is dated Fort Lewis, Washington, April 18 and reads in part as follows:
Brig. John Rockingham said today Canadian casualties in Korea likely will be higher than they were in Italy and Normandy.
He told a press conference on the eve of the 6,000-man force's departure from nearby Seattle for Korea that if a commonwealth division is formed in Korea, Canada might have to send additional troops to that war theatre.
When one bears in mind the reports that you have, Mr. Chairman, as to what I might call generally sanitary conditions in Korea,
I think it is highly likely that what Brigadier Rockingham said will be realized, taking into account the non-battle casualties alone; and, these, as the figures I have placed on the record will show, are equal to, if not greater than, the battle casualties, but they have just as great an effect from the point of view of wastage of forces. If then approximately half the average strength in Italy were nonbattle casualties during the course of a year, and if with battle casualties included your average rate was 61 per thousand per month for Italy, and with the likelihood that it will be higher in Korea, then I suggest these figures show that we need to take a second look at the manpower problem confronting
CMr. Fulton.]

this country in the light of the present program outlined by the government and the commitments which we have accepted.
We cannot afford to say to ourselves: "Let us not get excited, because this is peacetime; we cannot put forth an all-out effort." I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that we shall be doing a disservice to the country, a disservice to the men who are fighting in the forces now, and a disservice to those whom we are asking to volunteer if we do not face these facts and have a full and frank discussion of the implication of these facts, and we shall be horribly guilty if we ever again run even the risk of a situation arising where men are committed to battle and we suddenly find we have not got the resources, nor have we planned and prepared to have the resources in manpower immediately available adequately to maintain these troops, we simply cannot take that risk, because men are now fighting and dying in Korea. Also bear in mind this, which I will refer to again in a few moments -we are asking men to enlist to go to Europe. There is no fighting in Europe at the moment, but these men will have to be ready to meet an enemy, and a fully trained enemy, at any moment. That is why they are being sent there. This house is not entitled to regard the recruiting of a brigade for Europe as merely another aspect of a peacetime army. That brigade is being trained and raised to send to Europe to take its place in the line with our allies in the North Atlantic organization, ready to resist aggression at a moment's notice-<and a moment's notice is all they will have if the Russians should ever make the fatal decision to start the next world war.
When we look at our figures of recruiting I do not think we can find there a basis which would even entitle us to agree with the minister that the recruiting figures show that his program of 115,000 men in the three forces will be completed in a year and a half. The minister drew that conclusion from the figures of recruiting at the present time. It seems to me they show it would take over two years at the best, because although it is true enough that during January, February, March and April the average increase in the three services was over 2,000 a month, it is significant to note that during the month of April the intake was substantially less than it was during the previous month. It is also significant to note that it was higher in January, less in February and it was less again in March. The net intake for April, or an estimate of it, was given by the minister in his statement on May 8, and we find that the estimated over-all increase for that month was still less than it was the previous month.

Let us look at the trend. In January the net increase of the three services was 2,642. For February it was 2,173; for March it was 2,075. Does the minister remember what the figure for April was?
It was 1,934.

For April the estimated
increase was 1,934. Therefore the figures show a steady decline during the first four months. I realize that does not take into account the increase which will certainly be shown as a result of the announcement of the drive to recruit a special brigade for Europe, but the over-all trend was down steadily. That, Mr. Chairman, is a trend that will have to be reckoned with. That of course is the normal trend with respect to recruiting in the forces; that the winter months are the high months. Then, as we get toward the summer, they decrease, and particularly in the case of this country we must accept that, with the competing claims of industrial defence production, and particularly as that program is stepped up, there will be a tendency toward a greater increase in the downward trend of the recruiting figure.
Even if we take it that the average of
2,000	a month will be maintained, which seems to me to be making an estimate at a higher figure than the circumstances justify, when the minister made his announcement on February 5 we had 50,000 personnel to raise for the three services in order to achieve the program'-fifty thousand at the rate of 2,000 a month. Even if that rate were maintained it would thus take 25 months to reach the objective, or just over two years. Therefore I cannot see that the figures, as they are at the present time, justify the minister's anticipation that the program will be completed in a year and a half.
Furthermore, when one looks at the experience of the Korean brigade, which shows that approximately something over 10 per cent of the new recruitment had to be discharged or released even before the brigade ever left the continent, it certainly shows that the present recruiting policy and the policy of suddenly rushing into recruiting drives and putting pressure on is not an efficient one, is not the way in which any country should approach this problem of raising forces, because it is unscientific and' unsafe, because it is inefficient and expensive.
All this, Mr. Chairman, leads me to the conclusion that we need to take a second look at our manpower policy. I certainly wish to support the suggestion that has been made in this debate by one or two speakers
Supply-National Defence who preceded me, namely, that we need right now a national registration put into effect in this country.
The minister has said that we have a three-year program, but he himself has admitted that it does not rest with us to determine whether we shall have three years to complete that program. It rests with the Russians, who are the only potential aggressors. The implications as to whether or not we are going to be able to fulfil our commitments within the present limitation of
115,000	for the forces-I have dealt with the implications inherent in that problem-the implications inherent in the question of reinforcements and the rate of casualties in Korea, the implications inherent in the necessity to rotate the brigades in Europe and Korea, and the eleven squadrons of air force in Europe, plus the implications inherent in the tremendously high proportion of discharges from the Korean force, even before they left this country, particularly when this is reinforced by the fact and sober realization that we may not have three years, but may have only three months or less- all these implications, it seems to me, point inescapably to the conclusion that we must prepare now to meet the worst. And the only way we can prepare to meet the worst is by having a survey of our manpower, by national registration, and by preparation now to put into effect those measures to raise the forces which I believe may be necessary even without an act of aggression by Russia, but which will certainly become necessary the moment Russia commits an act of aggression,
Mr. Chairman, my own view as to the only proper, the fair and the safe way in which to raise a force to go into battle has been expressed already, and I think it does not need amplification. I am now trying to approach the problem within the limitations of the program laid down by the government, and trying to show that within the limitations of their own program it is necessary for them to take a second look at the whole problem.
I think that can be seen in a clearer light when we examine the methods now being followed to raise the brigade for Europe. In my view the wrong method of recruiting is being followed. I do not consider it fair to ask men to volunteer to discharge a national duty. I do not consider it fair, nor do I consider it safe or efficient. And I press this again, particularly in view of the fact that these men are asked to go to Europe to take their places in the line, where they may be called upon to meet a highly trained and ruthless enemy at any time.

Supply-National Defence
I have already referred to the example of the inefficiency which was necessarily inherent in the sudden, rushed and unscientific recruitment for the Korean brigade. Let me make it perfectly clear that I believe absolutely, and I am happy to believe, that the Korean brigade as it finally sailed for Korea was among the most efficient and most splendid, if not the most efficient and splendid that had ever been raised in this country- but at what a tremendous cost, in the matter of weeding out men who should never have been allowed to join it in the first place, as the result of a haphazard program of recruitment!
As I have said, these men are being asked to face the possibility of imminent war in Europe. I do not consider the method being followed of raising the brigade is the fair, the safe or the efficient way. Then, apart from that question, there are one or two other features of the present method of recruiting the brigade for Europe which, I suggest, should be examined. I realize it was extremely difficult to find a satisfactory compromise between the various factors the minister outlined for us when he announced the method to be followed in recruiting that brigade, having as a basis the reserve units across the country. He said we had to have a compromise between choosing three main units only and getting proper geographic representation. Those were among the factors considered.
The decision was arrived at to raise three battalions, one of which would1 be a highland battalion, one a straight infantry battalion and one a rifle battalion, and to give fifteen various reserve units the opportunity to recruit men for that brigade. As I understood the minister's statement, one of the advantages which were to flow from this method was the preservation of the regimental spirit-an objective with which I agree one hundred per cent.
But I think we should consider seriously whether in fact the method being followed will not actually defeat the objective. I wonder if it is going to be possible, when we have five different companies in a battalion wearing, as I understand they will wear, different regimental insignia. That is to say, a company of the Canadian Highland Regiment recruited by the Seaforth Highlanders would wear insignia different from a company recruited from the Canadian Scottish-that was my understanding, and I would ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong.
Shoulder badges.

Different shoulder badges-it
does seem to me it will be very difficult


when there are companies within a unit competing, as it were, on the basis of prior regimental affiliations, to build up a unit spirit, such as our whole Canadian army tradition has shown is so important and counts for so much in the winning of battles. Because not only will companies now have that proper spirit of competition and rivalry based upon a competitive spirit as between, let us say, A company and B company, but there will be the other aspect introduced when it will be pointed' out that A company used to be a company of Seaforth Highlanders whereas B company was Canadian Scottish.
Then there is the problem of transferring from one company to another within the same unit. The person involved would have to take down one set of shoulder flashes and put up another. It seems to me this would create a situation wherein the unit commander would find it exceedingly difficult to build up a proper unit spirit.
Then in addition we have the condition the minister outlined whereby other reserve force units will be asked to recruit reinforcement companies for the brigade, thus, as I understood him, further achieving the desired objective of maintaining the unit spirit and the regimental tradition. Again I believe the practice will defeat the objective. Because it seems to me that with a company of reinforcements raised by a battalion which is not a component company of the initial battalion of the brigade, and presumably wearing the shoulder flashes and the regimental insignia of their own unit during the time of their formation, coming into the battalion of the brigade and having to join companies with shoulder flashes different from that of the parent battalion of the reinforcement company, chaos and confusion would result, as well as a distinct feeling of let-down by the men, when they came in as members of X regiment and were then sent to one of the companies of the particular regiment and had to put up some other type of insignia.
